Sugar terraces climbing out of the sea, and the first landfall on every southbound voyage.
Anchored in 20 fathoms. Fair holding. It would be no place to lie in an onshore blow.
Water and provisions to be had here.
The people are Portuguese, and speak Português.
They have Sugar here, and plenty of it.

patent.title: The turn of the sea
patent.narrative: A short run and an easy one, and the Casa gives it to men it has not made up its mind about. Madeira is five hundred miles south-west and the north-easterly will put you there in a week without your having to think about it. Load sugar. Then come home by way of Terceira, in the Azores, which is eight hundred miles to the north-west of Madeira and in the wrong direction entirely — because the wind that carried you down will not carry you back, and the pilots of the Casa will tell you that the way home from the south is out into the ocean until the wind changes hands, and that a man who has not done it does not believe them. Go and do it. Then you will be trusted with the Guinea run.

log.text: A merchant speaks of a town some 19 days' sail to the south, of the Edo of Benin, with a king in it and a harbour. He had it from his brother, who trades that way.
The São Cristóvão lies in the Tagus, stored and watered. Whatever happens after this is written in this book.
Took the King’s charge: the Guinea run, to Mina and home.
Laid off a course for Funchal.
Bought 60 piece of panos de lã at 3.2 the piece, 195 cruzados in all. Good.
Watered and victualled for 90 days at a cost of 26 cruzados.
Practice has made you better at leadership: 1 point to spend.
Weighed and made sail. Wind 344° NNW, 12 knots.
Laid off a course for Mark.

The pilot: "Mind the tide here, senhor. It makes and takes 3.2 metres twice a day in this water, and every sounding you get is that much of a lie unless you know what the water is doing when you get it. It is half flood now, and high water in 2h24."

Ran the coast in sight all forenoon. It is on the Lisbon chart, but on it the way a thing is when nobody who drew it had been there — a line copied from a line. It is ours now, with a pilot’s name against it.
Made Mark, and shaped a course for Mark: 4 marks left of the passage.
Noon. 34 miles made good in the 6 hours since she sailed, latitude 38° 29.1' N by the reckoning. 40 miles still to run for Mark.
Noon. 128 miles made good in the twenty-four hours, latitude 37° 02.5' N by the reckoning. A fair day’s work. 391 miles still to run for Mark.
Dusk bell. the pilot's doubt has grown to 30 miles. The clock is down to four times.
Noon. 119 miles made good in the twenty-four hours, latitude 35° 25.0' N by the reckoning. A fair day’s work. 277 miles still to run for Mark.
Word from Lisbon: Diogo Cão has returned in the São Cristóvão of Lagos and reported Mpinda. The court has entered it on the padrão real under his name.
The hands took a shoal of dorado under the bow — 3 days of fresh meat for all hands.
Noon. 112 miles made good in the twenty-four hours, latitude 33° 58.3' N by the reckoning. A fair day’s work. 174 miles still to run for Mark.
The water has changed colour: greener than it was, and the lead finds a bottom.
Noon. 123 miles made good in the twenty-four hours, latitude 32° 31.1' N by the reckoning. A fair day’s work. 63 miles still to run for Mark.
Dusk bell. the pilot's doubt has grown to 51 miles. The clock is down to four times.
Made Mark, and shaped a course for Mark: 2 marks left of the passage.
Made Mark, and shaped a course for Funchal: 1 mark left of the passage.
A flight of boobies went over, all on the same course, heading lee. There is land that way, and not far.
Noon. 123 miles made good in the twenty-four hours, latitude 31° 56.2' N by the reckoning. A fair day’s work. 43 miles still to run for Funchal.
Noon. 47 miles made good in the twenty-four hours, latitude 32° 19.1' N by the reckoning. Poor. The hands have noticed. 19 miles still to run for Funchal.
Stood on as she was heading. The pilot said nothing, loudly.
Noon. 56 miles made good in the twenty-four hours, latitude 32° 37.9' N by the reckoning. Poor. The hands have noticed. 1 miles still to run for Funchal.
Noon. 128 miles made good in the twenty-four hours, latitude 32° 38.1' N by the reckoning. A fair day’s work. 1 miles still to run for Funchal.

Ran the coast in sight all forenoon. It is on the Lisbon chart, but on it the way a thing is when nobody who drew it had been there — a line copied from a line. It is ours now, with a pilot’s name against it.
Noon. 132 miles made good in the twenty-four hours, latitude 32° 38.1' N by the reckoning. A fair day’s work. 1 miles still to run for Funchal.

Raised the land 344° NNW after 10 days of blue water. No chart aboard shows anything here. The escrivão has been sent for. The pilot has her within a dozen miles and is saying so to anyone who will listen.
You steered straight for Funchal. The coast is up, and whether she lies north or south of us from here is a question the reckoning cannot answer to better than 3 miles. Somebody has to choose.
Margin on cargo at today's bids: +800 on 195 paid.
Spoilage: none.
Men lost: none.
Reckoning at landfall: 8 miles out.
Leg report, Lisboa to Funchal: 10 days against 8 on the Casa's reckoning (+2).

At Funchal, the island pilots talk of Ilha de São Brandão: it is seen from La Palma on clear evenings, and every ship that goes after it loses it in the haze. They put it about 29° north, 24° west, give or take 72 leagues. The pilot has pricked it on the chart with a question mark.
Came to an anchor off Funchal. Sugar terraces climbing out of the sea, and the first landfall on every southbound voyage.
Brás de Sousa, the master: “Sugar and wine, sir, and the last good water before the coast. Fill every cask.”

Opened a House at Funchal. Rui Correia is left in it with six men, ninety cruzados in the chest and the King’s commission, and he will be here when you come back or he will not. The berth aft is empty from today.
Bought the square-rigged caravel Espírito Santo for 1200 cruzados to run between Funchal and Lisboa.
